workflows.pain_point: Information is spread across multiple systems (GitHub, Confluence, Jira, internal documents) making it difficult to locate relevant information
workflows.current_process: Search across GitHub, Confluence, Jira, and internal documents
workflows.evidence: Michael: 'We also have information spread across GitHub, Confluence, Jira, and internal documents. Finding the right information is probably half the problem.'

workflows.pain_point: Documentation is often outdated and doesn't match actual implementation in code, requiring developers to search multiple systems and ask colleagues
workflows.current_process: Search Confluence, GitHub, Jira, and Slack; if answer not found, ask someone on the team who might know
workflows.evidence: Sneha: 'Usually we search Confluence, GitHub, Jira, and Slack. If we still can't find the answer, we ask someone on the team.' Daniel: 'And that's a problem because the person who knows the answer might be on another team or on leave.'

workflows.pain_point: Documentation is spread across multiple platforms (Confluence, GitHub, internal wikis) and finding specific answers takes much longer than asking an experienced engineer
workflows.current_process: Engineers search through Confluence, GitHub, and internal wikis to find relevant documentation
workflows.evidence: Sameer: 'There is documentation, but it's spread across Confluence, GitHub, and internal wikis. Some of it is useful, but it doesn't always explain how everything fits together.' Daniel: 'finding that answer in our documentation can take much longer.' Emily: 'We also have recorded training sessions, but people don't always know which ones are relevant to their role.'

workflows.workflow: Answering developer questions about AI policy compliance
workflows.pain_point: High volume of policy-related questions coming directly to Security team about whether specific engineering scenarios comply with AI usage policy
workflows.current_process: Developers ask Security team directly when unsure about AI tool usage; Security responds case-by-case
workflows.evidence: Faisal: 'We've received several questions about whether developers can use AI with production code, internal documentation, or data from customer systems.' Faisal: 'Fewer policy-related questions coming directly to Security and fewer cases where developers use the tool in ways that violate our guidelines.'

workflows.workflow: Interpreting AI usage policies for engineering scenarios
workflows.pain_point: Developers are interpreting general AI policy differently, leading to inconsistency; managers do not always know the approved answer when developers ask about specific use cases
workflows.current_process: Developers and managers attempt to interpret general AI policy on their own; ask managers or Security when unsure
workflows.frequency: Ongoing as developers encounter new scenarios
workflows.evidence: Faisal: 'We have a general AI policy, but it doesn't cover every engineering scenario. Developers are interpreting it differently.' Laura: 'I've had developers ask me whether they can use AI to analyze certain internal repositories. I don't always know what the approved answer is.'

workflows.pain_point: General AI policy does not cover every engineering scenario; need to define approved use cases, prohibited data, and escalation procedures
workflows.current_process: General AI policy exists but lacks engineering-specific scenarios and examples
workflows.evidence: Faisal: 'We have a general AI policy, but it doesn't cover every engineering scenario.' Faisal: 'A clear set of engineering-specific guidelines would help. We need to define approved use cases, prohibited data, and what developers should do when they're unsure.'

workflows.pain_point: Information is spread across several systems requiring manual gathering of context from logs, dashboards, deployments, Jira tickets, and previous incident reports before troubleshooting can begin
workflows.current_process: Engineers manually look through logs, dashboards, recent deployments, Jira tickets, and previous incident reports to gather context before starting troubleshooting
workflows.frequency: Several incidents every week across services
workflows.evidence: Kevin: 'A lot of the investigation is manual. We look through logs, dashboards, recent deployments, Jira tickets, and previous incident reports.' Arjun: 'An engineer might spend 30 or 40 minutes just gathering context before they start troubleshooting.' Kevin: 'We have several incidents every week across our services.'

workflows.workflow: Gathering incident context for unfamiliar services
workflows.pain_point: Engineers investigating incidents for services they haven't seen before need to understand the architecture and determine what changed, which is time-consuming
workflows.current_process: Engineers manually research service architecture and changes when investigating unfamiliar services
workflows.evidence: Lisa: 'The bigger problem is when the person investigating hasn't seen the service before. They need to understand the architecture and then figure out what changed.'

workflows.pain_point: Keeping documentation synchronized with code changes is difficult and manual process hasn't worked well
workflows.current_process: Manual documentation updates that are not consistently performed when code changes
workflows.evidence: Maria: 'We have talked about improving our documentation process, but keeping everything synchronized manually hasn't worked very well.' Daniel: 'It could also help generate documentation when a developer changes an API or introduces a new service.'

workflows.pain_point: Setup documentation gets outdated as dependencies change
workflows.current_process: Creating and manually maintaining setup documentation
workflows.evidence: Jonathan: 'We've created setup documentation, but it gets outdated as dependencies change.'

workflows.pain_point: New engineers need to learn architecture, services, development process, and internal tools, but documentation is spread across multiple systems and doesn't always explain how everything fits together
workflows.current_process: New engineers read documentation across Confluence, GitHub, and internal wikis, watch recorded training sessions, and ask experienced engineers questions
workflows.evidence: Emily: 'We hire engineers regularly, and getting them productive takes longer than we'd like.' Sameer: 'The biggest issue is that there's a lot they need to learn. They have to understand our architecture, services, development process, and internal tools.' Sameer: 'There is documentation, but it's spread across Confluence, GitHub, and internal wikis. Some of it is useful, but it doesn't always explain how everything fits together.'

workflows.pain_point: Experienced engineers spend significant time explaining technical concepts and architecture to new hires that could be documented, taking time away from other work
workflows.current_process: New engineers ask experienced engineers questions directly, and experienced engineers answer based on their knowledge
workflows.frequency: 2-4 hours per week during first month for each new hire
workflows.evidence: Daniel: 'When I joined, I spent a lot of time asking other engineers questions. Even now, when someone new joins my team, I spend several hours helping them understand the codebase.' Daniel: 'Probably two to four hours a week during the first month for each new hire.' Daniel: 'A new engineer might ask me, "How does the payments service communicate with the customer service?" I can explain it, but finding that answer in our documentation can take much longer.'

workflows.pain_point: Developers spend significant time installing dependencies, configuring services, getting credentials, and troubleshooting local environment issues with unhelpful error messages
workflows.current_process: Manually following setup documentation, searching Slack, GitHub issues, and old documentation to troubleshoot issues
workflows.frequency: New developers: almost every time; Existing developers: a few times a month when moving between services
workflows.evidence: Jonathan: 'New developers and even existing developers sometimes spend a surprising amount of time getting their local environment working.' Meera: 'Someone might spend half a day installing dependencies, configuring services, getting credentials, and figuring out why something isn't working locally.' Omar: 'For new developers, almost every time. For existing developers, probably a few times a month when they move between services.'

workflows.pain_point: Error messages aren't helpful and developers don't know whether issues stem from their machine, dependencies, or service configuration
workflows.current_process: Searching Slack, GitHub issues, and old documentation to find what others did to resolve similar issues
workflows.frequency: A few times a month for existing developers
workflows.evidence: Omar: 'And when something breaks, the error messages aren't always helpful. I usually search Slack, GitHub issues, and old documentation to figure out what someone else did.' Meera: 'The other problem is that developers often don't know whether the issue is with their machine, the dependency, or the service configuration.'

workflows.pain_point: Developers spend significant manual effort writing unit and regression tests after completing features, especially for older services
workflows.current_process: Developer finishes a feature and then manually writes unit and regression tests
workflows.frequency: Every sprint, sometimes more frequently when dealing with production bugs or larger releases
workflows.evidence: Alex: 'For some of the payments services, I'll finish a feature and then spend another couple of hours writing the unit and regression tests.' Mark: 'Testing is probably the biggest one for my team. Developers still spend a lot of time writing and updating tests manually, especially when we make changes to older services.'

workflows.pain_point: When codebase changes, developers must manually determine which existing tests are still relevant and add new ones, involving repetitive work
workflows.current_process: Developers figure out which existing tests are still relevant when something changes in the codebase and add new tests as needed
workflows.evidence: Mark: 'And it's not just writing the tests. When something changes in the codebase, we have to figure out which existing tests are still relevant and add new ones. A lot of that work is repetitive.'

workflows.pain_point: Senior engineers spend time reviewing tests created by junior developers rather than writing tests themselves
workflows.current_process: Senior engineers review tests created by junior developers
workflows.evidence: Mark: 'I'd estimate two to three hours per developer per sprint, although the senior engineers probably spend less time writing the tests themselves and more time reviewing what the junior developers create.'

workflows.pain_point: Engineers spend an hour or more figuring out what legacy code does before making changes, especially in older services written years ago that are no longer well understood
workflows.current_process: Search through repository, review old documentation, check Jira tickets, and ask colleagues who previously worked on the service
workflows.frequency: Several times a week across the team
workflows.evidence: Neha: 'When I get assigned an issue in one of the older Java services, I can spend an hour or more just figuring out what the code is doing before I can make a change.' Neha: 'Almost every time someone works on one of the older services. Maybe several times a week across the team.'

workflows.pain_point: Even experienced engineers must trace through several services to understand dependency chains
workflows.evidence: Michael: 'Even experienced engineers sometimes have to trace through several services before they understand the dependency chain.'

workflows.pain_point: Senior engineers spend significant time on routine code reviews, creating bottlenecks and preventing focus on architectural changes
workflows.current_process: All pull requests go through GitHub where one or two senior developers review, leave comments, developer makes changes, then PR returns for another review. Automated linting and static analysis are used but don't understand context of changes
workflows.frequency: High volume, particularly for smaller PRs
workflows.evidence: James: 'Code reviews are probably one of the bigger time sinks.' Rahul: 'we also get a lot of repetitive changes where I'm basically checking the same things over and over.' Ananya: 'The problem is that our senior developers are becoming a bottleneck. They need to review the important architectural changes, but they also spend a lot of time on routine reviews.'

workflows.pain_point: Engineers don't always know which runbook applies to the incident they are investigating
workflows.current_process: Runbooks exist but are not always followed because engineers don't know which one applies
workflows.evidence: Kevin: 'We have runbooks, but they're not always followed because engineers don't always know which runbook applies to the incident.'

workflows.pain_point: Engineers don't always know where to look in years of incident history to find similar past incidents
workflows.current_process: Manual search through incident history when engineers remember or discover similar incidents may exist
workflows.evidence: Kevin: 'It would also be useful if it could identify similar incidents we've had before. We have years of incident history but engineers don't always know where to look.'

workflows.pain_point: Developers discover documentation describes older versions only after following it, wasting time and causing confusion
workflows.current_process: Manual discovery when developers encounter mismatches between documentation and actual code implementation
workflows.evidence: Sneha: 'That's happened to me several times. I'll follow documentation to understand a service and then realize the documentation describes an older version.' Sneha: 'I'd be interested in something that could look at the code and existing documentation and identify where they don't match.'

workflows.pain_point: Manual gathering of information from Jira and GitHub, manually rewriting technical information for non-technical stakeholders, inconsistent formats across teams, time-consuming process
workflows.current_process: Developers and engineering managers manually go through tickets and pull requests each sprint, copy information from multiple Jira tickets into a document, rewrite technical content to make it understandable for product and business teams
workflows.frequency: Every sprint for smaller releases, less frequently for larger releases
workflows.evidence: Tom: 'The engineering teams have to gather information from Jira and GitHub and then prepare release notes for stakeholders.' Kavya: 'Every sprint we have developers and engineering managers going through tickets and pull requests to figure out what actually changed.' Chris: 'Sometimes I end up copying information from five or six Jira tickets into a document and then rewriting it so it makes sense.' Kavya: 'For a larger release, probably several hours across the team.'

workflows.pain_point: Engineers spend significant time understanding ticket context by reading Jira comments, related tickets, and searching for missing information before they can estimate or begin work
workflows.current_process: Engineers manually review Jira tickets, read comments, examine related tickets, search through previous tickets and Slack conversations, and schedule meetings with product managers when clarity is still lacking
workflows.evidence: Vikram: 'Sometimes I'll spend 30 minutes just understanding the context of a ticket before I can estimate it.' Aisha: 'Pretty much every planning cycle. Some tickets are clear, but a meaningful percentage need additional clarification.' Vikram: 'Usually I look through previous tickets or Slack conversations. If I still can't figure it out, I schedule time with the product manager.'

workflows.workflow: Training developers on AI security controls
workflows.pain_point: Telling developers to follow policy is not enough if they do not understand why controls exist; lack of clear examples reduces comfort with tool usage
workflows.current_process: Policy distributed to developers without context or training on rationale behind controls
workflows.frequency: Periodic or one-time per developer onboarding
workflows.evidence: Karen: 'I'd also like to see some form of training. Telling developers to follow a policy isn't enough if they don't understand why the controls exist.' Laura: 'If we had clear examples, developers would probably be more comfortable using the tool.'
